transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I’m Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… I suppose it’s work, mostly. I teach at the secondary school, and lately I just can’t shake this feeling that some of the staff emails and even the morning announcements are… not just ordinary messages. Like they’re coded, somehow, about me.

I know that sounds strange. My colleagues have shown me they were sent to everyone, very kindly, actually—one of them even printed the distribution list, which reminded me of when we used to do everything on paper in the staff room—but even then, I still feel like there’s something in the wording meant for me. It’s been bothering me enough that I thought I should come in.
Can you describe a specific example of something in the emails or announcements that you felt was directed at you? What made you think it was about you specifically?

Yes… one example was an email about staff needing to “maintain clear boundaries in communication” or something like that. Everyone said it was just a general reminder, and I know it went to the whole staff—someone even showed me the list—but the wording felt… pointed. Like “certain staff members” and “professional discretion,” those sorts of phrases. It made me think they were talking about me without saying my name.

And then the morning announcements—there was one about keeping the corridors quiet before registration, and I remember thinking, why that phrase, “quiet in the corridors,” because I’d walked through there earlier and—well, I used to supervise that corridor years ago, before they changed the timetable, which was a whole saga with the deputy head and the new bell system—but anyway, it felt like it was meant to tell me they’d noticed me. Even though, yes, technically everyone heard it.

Do you believe that these messages have been specifically designed to communicate something to you that others wouldn't understand, or that you were meant to pick up on something others weren't intended to notice?

Yes… I think that’s what frightens me a bit. Not that I think everyone is sitting in a room planning it exactly, but when those emails come through, or the announcements in the morning, I get this very strong feeling that there’s a second meaning in them. Like they’re ordinary for everyone else, but I’m meant to notice a bit underneath.

And I know my colleagues have been kind about it—they’ve shown me the messages went to everyone, and I do understand that, in a way. But I still can’t quite shake the feeling that certain phrases are about me. It’s like when you mark essays and you can tell a student is hinting at something without saying it outright—sorry, that’s probably not the best comparison, but that’s how it feels.
Have you had any other experiences where you felt certain about something being directed at you or having a special meaning that others don’t seem to notice?

Mostly it’s been the school messages, yes—the staff emails and the morning announcements. I can be sitting there with everyone else, and it’s meant to be routine, but I get this feeling that there’s something in it that I’m supposed to catch.

It’s odd, because I do know they’re sent to everyone. People have even shown me that, quite kindly. But certain phrases just sort of… stick out, and I can’t stop thinking they’re really about me. Like there’s a coded bit underneath the ordinary message. I suppose that’s the main thing that brought me in.
Have you ever felt that things in the world around you—like TV shows, music, or everyday conversations—also have hidden meanings that seem directed at you, even if others don’t notice it?

Not so much TV or music, no… I mean, I don’t sit at home watching the news thinking the presenter is talking to me or anything like that. It’s really been at school, with the staff emails and the morning announcements.

That’s why I came in, really, because I can’t seem to shake it. Even when my colleagues are very gentle and say, “Look, this went to everyone,” and they show me it’s a general email, I still feel certain phrases are… coded, I suppose. Like they’re about me without saying my name.

Everyday conversations—sometimes I might wonder if people are hinting, but the main thing is the school messages. The emails, the announcements. Those are the ones that feel directed at me.
Have you ever had any beliefs or thoughts that others have told you are not true or exaggerated, even though you felt certain they were real at the time?

Yes… I suppose that’s exactly it. My colleagues have told me I’m reading too much into the staff emails and the morning announcements, and they’ve been quite kind about it, really. They’ll say, “No, this was sent to everyone,” or show me the distribution list, which of course I understand on one level.

But at the time, it feels very real to me. Certain phrases just seem… placed there, if that makes sense. Like they’re not saying my name, but they’re meant for me to notice.

It sounds silly when I say it out loud. I used to tell my pupils to look for subtext in a poem, actually, and perhaps I’ve spent too many years doing that—sorry, that’s not really the point. The point is, yes, people have told me it’s exaggerated, but I still can’t quite shake the feeling that those messages are about me.
Can you think of a time when you were absolutely sure something was true, even though others told you it wasn’t possible or didn’t make sense?

Yes… the clearest example is the school emails and the morning announcements.

I can be told very calmly, “This went to everyone,” and I can see that it did, but there are certain phrases that just feel like they’ve been put there for me. Not openly, not with my name on it, but coded somehow. And I become quite sure of it in the moment.

It’s embarrassing, really, because I’m a teacher, I know how group messages work. I’ve sent enough of them myself—though usually mine are about homework deadlines or reminding Year 9 not to leave glue sticks without lids, which sounds trivial, but you’d be amazed how often it happens. Sorry… the point is, even when colleagues show me it’s ordinary, I still can’t shake the feeling that it’s about me.
Have you ever acted on any of these feelings or beliefs about the messages being directed at you—like confronting someone, changing your behavior significantly, or investigating the messages further?

I haven’t confronted anyone, no—not properly. I’ve come close to asking what they meant by a phrase in an email, but then I sort of… stop myself, because part of me knows it will sound strange.

Mostly I investigate it in my own head, I suppose. I reread the staff emails, compare them with the morning announcements, look for the wording that feels pointed at me. It’s a bit like when I’m marking essays and a pupil has repeated an image without realizing it—sorry, that’s not a very good comparison. But my mind does that pattern-matching thing.

I came in because I can’t seem to shake it, even when colleagues are gentle and show me it went to everyone. I don’t think I’ve changed anything dramatically, but I do find myself being more careful at school, wondering if something I do will be picked up in the next message.

Have you ever had any experiences where you believed something that others might consider completely impossible or not based in reality—something that you still felt certain was true even if there was no evidence for it?

Completely impossible… I don’t know if I’d put it quite that strongly. It’s not like I think the laws of nature have changed or anything like that.

It’s more that I become very certain that certain staff emails or morning announcements at school are coded messages about me. Even when people say, quite kindly, “No, everyone got that,” and they show me, I still feel there’s something in the wording that’s meant for me.

I know that must sound like reading too much into it. I did spend years teaching pupils to notice language and implication, and sometimes I think maybe my mind just won’t stop doing that—looking for subtext where there may not be any. But at the time it feels real, and that’s why I came in, really. I can’t seem to shake it.
Have you ever had a belief that something was happening or being directed at you in a way that would be considered impossible or not based in reality, even by people who know you well?

Yes… I think that’s what I mean, really. Not impossible like flying or anything, but not based in reality in the ordinary sense.

I came in because I can’t shake this feeling that certain staff emails, and sometimes the morning announcements at school, are really coded messages about me. Even when colleagues are very kind and show me, “Look, it went to everyone,” I still feel as if there’s a layer underneath it that’s aimed at me.

It’s the phrasing, usually. A word or a little sentence that catches at me. Which is ridiculous, because I spend half my life telling pupils not to over-interpret things unless they can support it with evidence—well, depending on the poem, of course, because sometimes ambiguity is the point. Sorry. But yes, people who know me would probably say that doesn’t make sense. I can see that, and still I feel it.

Have you ever had any other unusual beliefs or experiences—like thinking someone is watching you, sending you secret messages, or that you have special abilities—that others might find hard to believe or not based in reality?

Not special abilities, no—nothing like that. And I don’t think someone is literally watching me, exactly.

It’s more the messages. I know I’ve said this already, but that’s the thing I can’t get away from: certain staff emails, and sometimes the morning announcements, feel as if they’re coded and meant for me. A phrase will jump out, and then I’ll be thinking about it all day, the way you might keep turning over a line from a poem—though of course school emails are not poems, usually quite the opposite.

My colleagues have been kind. They’ll show me it was sent to everyone, and I do see that, on one level. But I still can’t shake the feeling there’s something underneath it, directed at me. That’s really why I came in.
Have you ever had moments where you felt that things in your environment were not what they seemed, even when there was no clear evidence to support that belief?

Yes, that’s a good way of putting it, I think — things not being what they seem.

At school especially, I’ll get a staff email, or hear one of the morning announcements, and on the surface it’s perfectly ordinary. Timetables, reminders, assemblies, that sort of thing. But then a phrase will sort of catch at me, and I’ll feel as if it’s actually about me, like there’s a coded message underneath it.

And I know people say, very reasonably, “No, everyone received that,” and they’ll even show me. I do understand that. But it doesn’t quite settle it in my mind. I still keep thinking, yes, but why that wording? Why say it that way?

It’s probably because I teach English, you know — you spend years telling children that word choice matters, and then suddenly every word seems to matter far too much. But yes, that’s the experience I’ve been having, and it’s hard to let go of even when there isn’t proper evidence.

Have you ever had any beliefs or experiences, outside of the school messages, where you felt certain something was true even when there was no evidence or others couldn't understand why you believed it?

Outside of school? I’m not sure, really… it’s mostly that. The emails, the announcements. That’s the bit that keeps catching me.

I mean, I can become very fixed on wording generally — occupational hazard, I suppose, teaching English for so long. I once spent an entire lesson arguing with Year 10 about whether “lonely” and “solitary” are the same thing, and of course they all just wanted the answer for the exam. But this is different from that.

With the school messages, I feel certain there’s something underneath them, something meant for me, even when people show me plainly that the email went to everyone. So outside of that, no… not really in the same way. It’s those messages that I can’t quite let go of.
Have you ever experienced any sensory perceptions—like seeing, hearing, or feeling things—that others around you don't seem to notice?

Yes… I suppose I have, though I haven’t been sure whether to mention it because it sounds rather dramatic when you say it out loud.

It’s usually when the house is quiet, or sometimes after the classroom has emptied and there’s that odd silence you get after a lesson — chairs scraping, bags, all of that gone. I’ll hear a woman’s voice say my name. Sometimes just my name, sometimes a little comment, like about what I’m doing. Clear enough that I’ll answer — actually answer — and then I realise there’s no one there.

It’s not all the time. And I did think at first, well, houses make noises, schools are full of echoes, and I’m getting older — though fifty-six is not ancient, whatever Year 11 may think. But it’s more like a voice than a creak or someone in the corridor. It unsettles me.
Do you hear the voice you mentioned even when you aren't reading an email or hearing an announcement from the school?

Yes — yes, it isn’t only when I’m reading an email or listening to the announcements.

It’s more often when everything’s gone quiet, actually. At home, if the house has settled, or after a class when the room’s emptied out — you know, that strange leftover quiet after thirty children have just been there and suddenly haven’t. I’ll hear a woman’s voice say my name, or sometimes just make a small comment about what I’m doing.

And it’s clear enough that I’ve answered before thinking. Then I look up and realise there’s no one there, which is… embarrassing, really, even if no one sees it. It’s not tied to the school messages in that moment, no.

doctor.question: Have you ever had any experiences where you believed something that others might consider completely impossible or not based in reality—something that you still felt certain was true even if there was no evidence for it?

patient.answer:
Completely impossible… I don’t know if I’d put it quite that strongly. It’s not like I think the laws of nature have changed or anything like that.

It’s more that I become very certain that certain staff emails or morning announcements at school are coded messages about me. Even when people say, quite kindly, “No, everyone got that,” and they show me, I still feel there’s something in the wording that’s meant for me.

I know that must sound like reading too much into it. I did spend years teaching pupils to notice language and implication, and sometimes I think maybe my mind just won’t stop doing that—looking for subtext where there may not be any. But at the time it feels real, and that’s why I came in, really. I can’t seem to shake it.

doctor.question: Have you ever had a belief that something was happening or being directed at you in a way that would be considered impossible or not based in reality, even by people who know you well?

target_item.name: Delusions

target_item.reason: The question is asking about a fixed belief that events or messages are being directed at the patient despite others considering it not based in reality, which matches the delusions profile.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think that’s what I mean, really. Not impossible like flying or anything, but not based in reality in the ordinary sense.

I came in because I can’t shake this feeling that certain staff emails, and sometimes the morning announcements at school, are really coded messages about me. Even when colleagues are very kind and show me, “Look, it went to everyone,” I still feel as if there’s a layer underneath it that’s aimed at me.

It’s the phrasing, usually. A word or a little sentence that catches at me. Which is ridiculous, because I spend half my life telling pupils not to over-interpret things unless they can support it with evidence—well, depending on the poem, of course, because sometimes ambiguity is the point. Sorry. But yes, people who know me would probably say that doesn’t make sense. I can see that, and still I feel it.

doctor.question: Have you ever had any other unusual beliefs or experiences—like thinking someone is watching you, sending you secret messages, or that you have special abilities—that others might find hard to believe or not based in reality?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about unusual fixed beliefs such as secret messages, being watched, or special abilities that others would see as not based in reality.

patient.answer:
Not special abilities, no—nothing like that. And I don’t think someone is literally watching me, exactly.

It’s more the messages. I know I’ve said this already, but that’s the thing I can’t get away from: certain staff emails, and sometimes the morning announcements, feel as if they’re coded and meant for me. A phrase will jump out, and then I’ll be thinking about it all day, the way you might keep turning over a line from a poem—though of course school emails are not poems, usually quite the opposite.

My colleagues have been kind. They’ll show me it was sent to everyone, and I do see that, on one level. But I still can’t shake the feeling there’s something underneath it, directed at me. That’s really why I came in.

There is no evidence of hallucinations or more broadly disorganized thinking, and no indication of other symptom clusters (e.g., mood episodes, autism spectrum features). The differential remains delusional disorder (F22) and schizophrenia, paranoid type (F20), as the patient’s beliefs could represent either a circumscribed delusional system or an early/attenuated manifestation of schizophrenia.

doctor.question: Have you ever had moments where you felt that things in your environment were not what they seemed, even when there was no clear evidence to support that belief?

patient.answer:
Yes, that’s a good way of putting it, I think — things not being what they seem.

At school especially, I’ll get a staff email, or hear one of the morning announcements, and on the surface it’s perfectly ordinary. Timetables, reminders, assemblies, that sort of thing. But then a phrase will sort of catch at me, and I’ll feel as if it’s actually about me, like there’s a coded message underneath it.

And I know people say, very reasonably, “No, everyone received that,” and they’ll even show me. I do understand that. But it doesn’t quite settle it in my mind. I still keep thinking, yes, but why that wording? Why say it that way?

It’s probably because I teach English, you know — you spend years telling children that word choice matters, and then suddenly every word seems to matter far too much. But yes, that’s the experience I’ve been having, and it’s hard to let go of even when there isn’t proper evidence.

inference.note: The patient continues to describe experiences consistent with delusional thinking, specifically referential delusions related to staff emails and announcements. There is no evidence of hallucinations or more widespread delusional themes, which supports the persistence of F22 (Delusional Disorder) as a candidate. The possibility of Schizophrenia (F20) remains due to the presence of delusions, but the lack of characteristic negative symptoms, disorganization, or functional decline makes it less likely at this point. doctor.question: Have you ever had any beliefs or experiences, outside of the school messages, where you felt certain something was true even when there was no evidence or others couldn't understand why you believed it?

patient.answer:
Outside of school? I’m not sure, really… it’s mostly that. The emails, the announcements. That’s the bit that keeps catching me.

I mean, I can become very fixed on wording generally — occupational hazard, I suppose, teaching English for so long. I once spent an entire lesson arguing with Year 10 about whether “lonely” and “solitary” are the same thing, and of course they all just wanted the answer for the exam. But this is different from that.

With the school messages, I feel certain there’s something underneath them, something meant for me, even when people show me plainly that the email went to everyone. So outside of that, no… not really in the same way. It’s those messages that I can’t quite let go of.

inference.note: The patient continues to describe experiences consistent with delusional thinking, specifically focused on school-related communications having hidden, personal meanings. There is no evidence of generalized delusions, hallucinations, or other prominent psychotic features, which supports the continued consideration of F22 (Delusional Disorder). F20 (Schizophrenia) remains less likely due to the absence of hallmark symptoms such as formal thought disorder, hallucinations, or negative symptoms. No new information has ruled out either diagnosis definitively.

doctor.question: Have you ever experienced any sensory perceptions—like seeing, hearing, or feeling things—that others around you don't seem to notice?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about sensory perceptions such as hearing or seeing things that others do not notice, which directly matches hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Yes… I suppose I have, though I haven’t been sure whether to mention it because it sounds rather dramatic when you say it out loud.

It’s usually when the house is quiet, or sometimes after the classroom has emptied and there’s that odd silence you get after a lesson — chairs scraping, bags, all of that gone. I’ll hear a woman’s voice say my name. Sometimes just my name, sometimes a little comment, like about what I’m doing. Clear enough that I’ll answer — actually answer — and then I realise there’s no one there.

It’s not all the time. And I did think at first, well, houses make noises, schools are full of echoes, and I’m getting older — though fifty-six is not ancient, whatever Year 11 may think. But it’s more like a voice than a creak or someone in the corridor. It unsettles me.

inference.note: The patient reported auditory hallucinations (e.g., hearing a voice call their name in the absence of external stimuli), which supports the persistence of F20 (Schizophrenia) as a candidate. The delusional interpretation of ordinary messages as having special, personal significance (delusional perception) also continues to support F22 (Delusional Disorder). No further information has ruled out either diagnosis at this time.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's reported auditory experiences meet criteria for hallucinations, and whether they occur independently of the perceived coded messages.
doctor.question: Do you hear the voice you mentioned even when you aren't reading an email or hearing an announcement from the school?

patient.answer:
Yes — yes, it isn’t only when I’m reading an email or listening to the announcements.

It’s more often when everything’s gone quiet, actually. At home, if the house has settled, or after a class when the room’s emptied out — you know, that strange leftover quiet after thirty children have just been there and suddenly haven’t. I’ll hear a woman’s voice say my name, or sometimes just make a small comment about what I’m doing.

And it’s clear enough that I’ve answered before thinking. Then I look up and realise there’s no one there, which is… embarrassing, really, even if no one sees it. It’s not tied to the school messages in that moment, no.
